peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: When I examine myself, Seneca, some vices appear on the surface, and so that I can lay my hands upon them, while others are less distinct and harder to reach, and some are not always present, but recur at intervals: and these I should call the most troublesome, being like a roving enemy that assails one when he sees his opportunity, and who will neither let one stand on one's guard as in war, nor yet take one's rest without fear as in peace. The position in which I find myself more especially (for why should I not tell you the truth as I would to a physician), is that of neither being thoroughly set free from the vices which I fear and hate, nor yet quite in bondage to them: my state of mind, though not the worst possible, is a particularly discontented and sulky one: I am neither ill nor well.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: When I look at myself, Seneca, some of my flaws are obvious and easy to spot. I can get my hands on them. But others are harder to see and reach. And some don't stay around all the time — they come and go. These are the most annoying ones. They're like an enemy that attacks whenever they see a chance. They won't let me stay on guard like I'm at war, but they also won't let me rest easy like I'm at peace. Here's my situation (and why shouldn't I tell you the truth, like I would tell a doctor): I'm not completely free from the vices I fear and hate, but I'm not completely trapped by them either. My state of mind isn't the worst it could be, but it's particularly frustrated and moody. I'm neither sick nor healthy.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: It is of no use for you to tell me that all virtues are weakly at the outset, and that they acquire strength and solidity by time, for I am well aware that even those which do but help our outward show, such as grandeur, a reputation for eloquence, and everything that appeals to others, gain power by time. Both those which afford us real strength and those which do but trick us out in a more attractive form, require long years before they gradually are adapted to us by time. But I fear that custom, which confirms most things, implants this vice more and more deeply in me. Long acquaintance with both good and bad people leads one to esteem them all alike.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: Don't tell me that all virtues start weak and grow stronger over time. I already know that. Even shallow things like status, reputation for speaking well, and anything else meant to impress others get more powerful with practice. Both the virtues that truly make us strong and the ones that just make us look good need years to become part of who we are. But I'm afraid that habit, which makes most things stick, is driving this flaw deeper into me. When you spend a long time around both good and bad people, you start to see them all as the same.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: What this state of weakness really is, when the mind halts between two opinions without any strong inclination towards either good or evil, I shall be better able to show you piecemeal than all at once. I will tell you what befalls me, you must find out the name of the disease. I have to confess the greatest possible love of thrift: I do not care for a bed with gorgeous hangings, nor for clothes brought out of a chest, or pressed under weights and made glossy by frequent manglings, but for common and cheap ones, that require no care either to keep them or to put them on. For food I do not want what needs whole troops of servants to prepare it and admire it, nor what is ordered many days before and served up by many hands, but something handy and easily come at, with nothing far-fetched or costly about it, to be had in every part of the world, burdensome neither to one's fortune nor one's body, not likely to go out of the body by the same path by which it came in.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I can show you what this mental weakness looks like better through specific examples than by explaining it all at once. Let me tell you what happens to me, and you can figure out what to call this condition. I have to admit I love being frugal. I don't want a bed with fancy decorations or clothes that come from some special chest — clothes that have been pressed with weights and made shiny through constant ironing. I prefer simple, cheap things that don't need special care to store or wear. For food, I don't want dishes that require armies of servants to prepare and fuss over, or meals that must be ordered days ahead and served by many hands. I want something simple and easy to get — nothing exotic or expensive. Food that's available anywhere in the world, that won't burden either my wallet or my body, and won't cause digestive problems.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: I like a rough and unpolished homebred servant, I like my servant born in my house: I like my country-bred father's heavy silver plate stamped with no maker's name: I do not want a table that is beauteous with dappled spots, or known to all the town by the number of fashionable people to whom it has successively belonged, but one which stands merely for use, and which causes no guest's eye to dwell upon it with pleasure or to kindle at it with envy. While I am well satisfied with this, I am reminded of the clothes of a certain schoolboy, dressed with no ordinary care and splendour, of slaves bedecked with gold and a whole regiment of glittering attendants. I think of houses too, where one treads on precious stones, and where valuables lie about in every corner, where the very roof is brilliantly painted, and a whole nation attends and accompanies an inheritance on the road to ruin.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I like a rough, unpolished servant who was born in my own house. I like my father's heavy silver plate from the countryside — the kind with no fancy maker's mark on it. I don't want a table that's beautiful with fancy wood patterns, or one that's famous around town because it belonged to a series of fashionable owners. I want a table that's just for use — one that doesn't make guests stare at it with pleasure or burn with envy. But even though I'm satisfied with this simple life, I can't help thinking about other things I've seen: a schoolboy dressed with extraordinary care and splendor, slaves covered in gold, and a whole army of glittering attendants. I think about houses where you walk on precious stones, where valuable things are scattered in every corner, where even the ceiling is brilliantly painted. I see a whole nation following along as an inheritance rushes toward ruin.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: What shall I say of waters, transparent to the very bottom, which flow round the guests, and banquets worthy of the theatre in which they take place? Coming as I do from a long course of dull thrift, I find myself surrounded by the most brilliant luxury, which echoes around me on every side: my sight becomes a little dazzled by it: I can lift up my heart against it more easily than my eyes. When I return from seeing it I am a sadder, though not a worse man, I cannot walk amid my own paltry possessions with so lofty a step as before, and silently there steals over me a feeling of vexation, and a doubt whether that way of life may not be better than mine. None of these things alter my principles, yet all of them disturb me.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: What can I say about those crystal-clear pools that flow around the dinner guests? Or about banquets so grand they belong on a stage? Coming from my simple, frugal life, I'm suddenly surrounded by dazzling luxury everywhere I look. My eyes can barely take it in. I find it easier to resist with my mind than with my sight. When I come home afterward, I'm sadder but not worse as a person. I can't walk through my own humble things with the same confidence as before. A quiet irritation creeps over me, along with doubts about whether their way of living might actually be better than mine. These experiences don't change my beliefs, but they definitely shake me up.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: At one time I would obey the maxims of our school and plunge into public life, I would obtain office and become consul, not because the purple robe and lictor's axes attract me, but in order that I may be able to be of use to my friends, my relatives, to all my countrymen, and indeed to all mankind. Ready and determined, I follow the advice of Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus, all of whom bid one take part in public affairs, though none of them ever did so himself: and then, as soon as something disturbs my mind, which is not used to receiving shocks, as soon as something occurs which is either disgraceful, such as often occurs in all men's lives, or which does not proceed quite easily, or when subjects of very little importance require me to devote a great deal of time to them, I go back to my life of leisure, and, just as even tired cattle go faster when they are going home, I wish to retire and pass my life within the walls of my house.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: Sometimes I follow my school's teachings and throw myself into public life. I seek office and aim to become consul — not because I want the purple robes or the power, but because I want to help my friends, my family, my fellow citizens, and all humanity. I feel ready and determined. I follow the advice of Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus, who all tell us to take part in politics. (Though none of them actually did it themselves.) But then something upsets my mind, which isn't used to being shocked. Maybe something disgraceful happens — the kind of thing that happens in everyone's life. Or things don't go smoothly. Or trivial matters demand way too much of my time. So I retreat back to my private life. Like tired cattle who walk faster when they're heading home, I want to retire and spend my life within my own walls.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: "No one," I say, "that will give me no compensation worth such a loss shall ever rob me of a day. Let my mind be contained within itself and improve itself: let it take no part with other men's affairs, and do nothing which depends on the approval of others: let me enjoy a tranquillity undisturbed by either public or private troubles." But whenever my spirit is roused by reading some brave words, or some noble example spurs me into action, I want to rush into the law courts, to place my voice at one man's disposal, my services at another's, and to try to help him even though I may not succeed, or to quell the pride of some lawyer who is puffed up by ill-deserved success: but I think, by Hercules, that in philosophical speculation it is better to view things as they are, and to speak of them on their own account, and as for words, to trust to things for them, and to let one's speech simply follow whither they lead.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I tell myself: "No one who can't give me something truly valuable in return will ever steal a day from me. Let my mind focus on itself and grow stronger. Let it stay out of other people's business and do nothing that depends on their approval. Let me enjoy peace that isn't disturbed by public drama or private troubles." But then I read something inspiring or see a noble example, and suddenly I want to rush to the courthouse. I want to lend my voice to one person, my help to another. I want to try to help someone even if I might fail, or put down some arrogant lawyer who's gotten too big for his boots from success he doesn't deserve. But honestly, I think it's better in philosophy to see things as they really are and speak about them plainly. Trust the subject matter to provide the words, and let your speech simply follow where the ideas lead.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: "Why do you want to construct a fabric that will endure for ages? Do you not wish to do this in order that posterity may talk of you: yet you were born to die, and a silent death is the least wretched. Write something therefore in a simple style, merely to pass the time, for your own use, and not for publication. Less labour is needed when one does not look beyond the present." Then again, when the mind is elevated by the greatness of its thoughts, it becomes ostentatious in its use of words, the loftier its aspirations, the more loftily it desires to express them, and its speech rises to the dignity of its subject. At such times I forget my mild and moderate determination and soar higher than is my wont, using a language that is not my own.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: Why do you want to create something that will last forever? You want future generations to remember you. But you were born to die, and a quiet death is actually the least painful kind. So just write something simple to pass the time. Write for yourself, not for others to read. It's much easier when you only focus on today. But then again, when your mind gets excited by big ideas, it starts showing off with fancy words. The grander your thoughts, the more grandly you want to express them. Your writing style rises to match your subject. When this happens, I forget my plan to stay calm and reasonable. I soar higher than usual, using language that doesn't sound like me.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: Not to multiply examples, I am in all things attended by this weakness of a well-meaning mind, to whose level I fear that I shall be gradually brought down, or, what is even more worrying, that I may always hang as though about to fall, and that there may be more the matter with me than I myself perceive: for we take a friendly view of our own private affairs, and partiality always obscures our judgment. I fancy that many men would have arrived at wisdom had they not believed themselves to have arrived there already, had they not purposely deceived themselves as to some parts of their character, and passed by others with their eyes shut: for you have no grounds for supposing that other people's flattery is more ruinous to us than our own. Who dares to tell himself the truth? Who is there, by however large a troop of caressing courtiers he may be surrounded, who in spite of them is not his own greatest flatterer?
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I could give more examples, but the point is clear: I struggle with this same weakness of having good intentions but poor execution. I worry that I'll gradually sink to this level of mediocrity. Or worse — that I'll always be on the verge of falling, with deeper problems than I even realize. We view our own private lives through rose-colored glasses. Bias always clouds our judgment. I think many people would have reached wisdom if they hadn't convinced themselves they were already wise. They lie to themselves about parts of their character and deliberately ignore other flaws. Don't assume that other people's flattery hurts us more than our own self-deception. Who has the courage to tell himself the truth? No matter how many fawning admirers surround someone, isn't he still his own biggest flatterer?

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText: I beg you, therefore, if you have any remedy by which you could stop this vacillation of mine, to deem me worthy to owe my peace of mind to you. I am well aware that these oscillations of mind are not perilous and that they threaten me with no serious disorder: to express what I complain of by an exact simile, I am not suffering from a storm, but from sea-sickness. Take from me, then, this evil, whatever it may be, and help one who is in distress within sight of land.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: So please, if you have any cure that could stop this back-and-forth in my mind, I would be grateful to owe you my peace. I know these mental swings aren't dangerous and won't cause any serious harm. To put it exactly: I'm not caught in a storm, but I am seasick. Whatever this problem is, please take it away from me. Help someone who is struggling even though he can see the shore.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: I have long been silently asking myself, my friend Serenus, to what I should liken such a condition of mind, and I find that nothing more closely resembles it than the conduct of those who, after having recovered from a long and serious illness, occasionally experience slight touches and twinges, and, although they have passed through the final stages of the disease, yet have suspicions that it has not left them, and though in perfect health yet hold out their pulse to be felt by the physician, and whenever they feel warm suspect that the fever is returning.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: I've been thinking for a long time, my friend Serenus, about how to describe this state of mind. The best comparison I can find is this: some people recover from a long, serious illness. But even after they're completely well, they still feel little aches and pains. They worry the disease might come back. They're perfectly healthy, but they keep asking doctors to check their pulse. Every time they feel warm, they panic that their fever is returning.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: What you desire, to be undisturbed, is a great thing, nay, the greatest thing of all, and one which raises a man almost to the level of a god. The Greeks call this calm steadiness of mind _euthymia_, and Democritus's treatise upon it is excellently written: I call it peace of mind: for there is no necessity for translating so exactly as to copy the words of the Greek idiom: the essential point is to mark the matter under discussion by a name which ought to have the same meaning as its Greek name, though perhaps not the same form. What we are seeking, then, is how the mind may always pursue a steady, unruffled course, may be pleased with itself, and look with pleasure upon its surroundings, and experience no interruption of this joy, but abide in a peaceful condition without being ever either elated or depressed: this will be "peace of mind." Let us now consider in a general way how it may be attained: then you may apply as much as you choose of the universal remedy to your own case.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: What you want — to be undisturbed — is a great thing. In fact, it's the greatest thing of all. It almost raises a person to the level of a god. The Greeks call this calm steadiness of mind _euthymia_. Democritus wrote an excellent treatise about it. I call it peace of mind. There's no need to translate so exactly that we copy Greek words. The important thing is to use a name that captures the same meaning, even if it takes a different form. So what we're looking for is this: how can the mind always follow a steady, untroubled path? How can it be pleased with itself and look with pleasure at what's around it? How can it experience no interruption of this joy, but stay in a peaceful state — never getting too high or too low? This is 'peace of mind.' Let's think about how to achieve it in general terms. Then you can apply as much of this universal remedy to your own situation as you want.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: Meanwhile we must drag to light the entire disease, and then each one will recognize his own part of it: at the same time you will understand how much less you suffer by your self-depreciation than those who are bound by some showy declaration which they have made, and are oppressed by some grand title of honour, so that shame rather than their own free will forces them to keep up the pretence.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: Meanwhile, we need to bring this whole problem out into the open. Then each person will see their own piece of it. You'll also realize how much better off you are with your self-doubt than those people who are trapped by some flashy promise they made or weighed down by some impressive title. Shame forces them to keep up the act, not their own choice.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: This arises from a distemperature of mind and from desires which one is afraid to express or unable to fulfil, when men either dare not attempt as much as they wish to do, or fail in their efforts and depend entirely upon hope: such people are always fickle and changeable, which is a necessary consequence of living in a state of suspense: they take any way to arrive at their ends, and teach and force themselves to use both dishonourable and difficult means to do so, so that when their toil has been in vain they are made wretched by the disgrace of failure, and do not regret having longed for what was wrong, but having longed for it in vain. They then begin to feel sorry for what they have done, and afraid to begin again, and their mind falls by degrees into a state of endless vacillation, because they can neither command nor obey their passions, of hesitation, because their life cannot properly develope itself, and of decay, as the mind becomes stupefied by disappointments.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: This restlessness comes from an unbalanced mind and desires that people are either afraid to admit or can't achieve. They don't dare try for what they really want, or they fail when they do try, so they live entirely on hope. These people are always changing their minds — which makes sense when you're constantly hanging in suspense. They'll use any method to get what they want. They force themselves to try shameful and difficult approaches. When all that effort fails, they feel miserable about the disgrace of failing. But they don't regret wanting the wrong things — they regret wanting them unsuccessfully. Then they feel sorry for what they've done and afraid to try again. Their minds fall into endless back-and-forth because they can't control their desires or give in to them. They hesitate because their lives can't develop properly. They decay as disappointment makes their minds numb.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: All these symptoms become aggravated when their dislike of a laborious misery has driven them to idleness and to secret studies, which are unendurable to a mind eager to take part in public affairs, desirous of action and naturally restless, because, of course, it finds too few resources within itself: when therefore it loses the amusement which business itself affords to busy men, it cannot endure home, loneliness, or the walls of a room, and regards itself with dislike when left to itself. Hence arises that weariness and dissatisfaction with oneself, that tossing to and fro of a mind which can nowhere find rest, that unhappy and unwilling endurance of enforced leisure.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: All these problems get worse when people hate the burden of hard work and retreat into laziness and private studies. But minds that crave public life and action can't stand this kind of isolation. They are naturally restless and don't have enough inner resources to sustain themselves. When they lose the entertainment that busy work provides, they can't bear being home, alone, or stuck in a room. They start to dislike themselves when left to their own company. This creates that exhausting self-dissatisfaction, that restless tossing back and forth of a mind that can't find peace anywhere. They become miserable prisoners of their own forced leisure.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: In all cases where one feels ashamed to confess the real cause of one's suffering, and where modesty leads one to drive one's sufferings inward, the desires pent up in a little space without any vent choke one another. Hence comes melancholy and drooping of spirit, and a thousand waverings of the unsteadfast mind, which is held in suspense by unfulfilled hopes, and saddened by disappointed ones: hence comes the state of mind of those who loathe their idleness, complain that they have nothing to do, and view the progress of others with the bitterest jealousy: for an unhappy sloth favours the growth of envy, and men who cannot succeed themselves wish every one else to be ruined.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: When you're too ashamed to admit what's really bothering you, and pride makes you keep your troubles locked inside, those buried feelings have nowhere to go. They pile up and choke each other out. This leads to depression and despair, and endless uncertainty in a mind torn between unfulfilled hopes and crushed expectations. This is why some people hate their own laziness but complain they have nothing to do. They watch others succeed with bitter jealousy. When you're miserable and idle, envy grows like a weed. People who can't succeed themselves want everyone else to fail too.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: This dislike of other men's progress and despair of one's own produces a mind angered against fortune, addicted to complaining of the age in which it lives, to retiring into corners and brooding over its misery, until it becomes sick and weary of itself: for the human mind is naturally nimble and apt at movement: it delights in every opportunity of excitement and forgetfulness of itself, and the worse a man's disposition the more he delights in this, because he likes to wear himself out with busy action, just as some sores long for the hands that injure them and delight in being touched, and the foul itch enjoys anything that scratches it.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: When we resent other people's success and lose hope in our own, we get angry at fate. We complain about the times we live in. We retreat into isolation and brood over our misery until we become sick of ourselves. The human mind naturally wants to move and stay busy. It loves any chance to get excited and forget itself. And the worse someone's character, the more they crave this kind of distraction. They like to exhaust themselves with frantic activity, the way infected wounds crave the hands that hurt them, or the way an itch enjoys being scratched.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: Similarly I assure you that these minds, over which desires have spread like evil ulcers, take pleasure in toils and troubles, for there are some things which please our body while at the same time they give it a certain amount of pain, such as turning oneself over and changing one's side before it is wearied, or cooling oneself in one position after another. It is like Homer's Achilles, lying first upon its face, then upon its back, placing itself in various attitudes, and, as sick people are wont, enduring none of them for long, and using changes as though they were remedies.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: I promise you this: minds that are eaten up by desires — like infected wounds — actually enjoy stress and trouble. Think about it. Some things feel good to your body even while they hurt a little. Like tossing and turning in bed, switching from side to side before you're even tired. Or shifting around to find a cool spot on the pillow. It's like Homer's Achilles — lying face down, then on his back, trying different positions. Sick people do this. They can't stand any position for long, so they keep changing, thinking the next position will be the cure.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
Hence men undertake aimless wanderings, travel along distant shores, and at one time at sea, at another by land, try to soothe that fickleness of disposition which always is dissatisfied with the present. "Now let us make for Campania: now I am sick of rich cultivation: let us see wild regions, let us thread the passes of Bruttii and Lucania: yet amid this wilderness one wants something of beauty to relieve our pampered eyes after so long dwelling on savage wastes: let us seek Tarentum with its famous harbour, its mild winter climate, and its district, rich enough to support even the great hordes of ancient times. Let us now return to town: our ears have too long missed its shouts and noise: it would be pleasant also to enjoy the sight of human bloodshed." Thus one journey succeeds another, and one sight is changed for another. As Lucretius says:—

"Thus every mortal from himself doth flee;"

but what does he gain by so doing if he does not escape from himself? he follows himself and weighs himself down by his own most burdensome companionship.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: This is why people take pointless trips. They wander to distant shores. They travel by sea, then by land. They're trying to calm that restless mind that's never happy with where it is. "Let's go to Campania! I'm tired of all this luxury — let's see some wild country. Let's hike through the mountains of Bruttii and Lucania. But wait, all this wilderness is getting boring. Our spoiled eyes need something beautiful after staring at wasteland for so long. Let's head to Tarentum — great harbor, mild winters, rich land that could feed vast armies back in the old days. Actually, let's go back to the city. I miss the noise and shouting. And it would be fun to watch some gladiator fights." One trip leads to another. One scene gets swapped for the next. As Lucretius said: "Every person runs away from himself." But what's the point? You can't escape yourself. You drag yourself along wherever you go, stuck with your own awful company.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText: We must understand, therefore, that what we suffer from is not the fault of the places but of ourselves: we are weak when there is anything to be endured, and cannot support either labour or pleasure, either one's own business or any one else's for long. This has driven some men to death, because by frequently altering their purpose they were always brought back to the same point, and had left themselves no room for anything new. They had become sick of life and of the world itself, and as all indulgences palled upon them they began to ask themselves the question, "How long are we to go on doing the same thing?"
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: We need to understand that our problems come from us, not from where we are. We are weak when we have to endure anything. We can't handle work or pleasure for very long. We can't stick with our own projects or other people's. This weakness has driven some people to kill themselves. They kept changing their plans but always ended up in the same place. They left no room for anything new in their lives. They got sick of life and the world itself. When all pleasures became boring, they started asking themselves: 'How long do we have to keep doing the same thing?'

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText: You ask me what I think we had better make use of to help us to support this ennui. "The best thing," as Athenodorus says, "is to occupy oneself with business with the management of affairs of state and the duties of a citizen: for as some pass the day in exercising themselves in the sun and in taking care of their bodily health, and athletes find it most useful to spend the greater part of their time in feeding up the muscles and strength to whose cultivation they have devoted their lives; so too for you who are training your mind to take part in the struggles of political life, it is far more honourable to be thus at work than to be idle.
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: You ask me what I think we should do to fight off this restless boredom. "The best remedy," as Athenodorus says, "is to stay busy with real work — managing public affairs and doing your duties as a citizen. Some people spend their days exercising in the sun and taking care of their bodies. Athletes find it most helpful to spend most of their time building up the muscles and strength they've dedicated their lives to developing. In the same way, if you're training your mind for the struggles of political life, it's much more honorable to be working than sitting around doing nothing.

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText: He whose object is to be of service to his countrymen and to all mortals, exercises himself and does good at the same time when he is engrossed in business and is working to the best of his ability both in the interests of the public and of private men. But," continues he, "because innocence is hardly safe among such furious ambitions and so many men who turn one aside from the right path, and it is always sure to meet with more hindrance than help, we ought to withdraw ourselves from the forum and from public life, and a great mind even in a private station can find room wherein to expand freely. Confinement in dens restrains the springs of lions and wild creatures, but this does not apply to human beings, who often effect the most important works in retirement.
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: The person who wants to serve his country and all people can practice virtue and do good at the same time when he's busy with public affairs. He works as hard as he can for both the public good and for private citizens. But," he continues, "it's hard to stay innocent when ambitions are so fierce and so many people try to lead you off the right path. You're sure to face more obstacles than help. So we should withdraw from the forum and from public life. Even a great mind can find room to flourish in private life. Putting lions and wild animals in cages restrains their energy, but this doesn't apply to humans. People often do their most important work in retirement.

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText: Let a man, however, withdraw himself only in such a fashion that wherever he spends his leisure his wish may still be to benefit individual men and mankind alike, both with his intellect, his voice, and his advice. The man that does good service to the state is not only he who brings forward candidates for public office, defends accused persons, and gives his vote on questions of peace and war, but he who encourages young men in well-doing, who supplies the present dearth of good teachers by instilling into their minds the principles of virtue, who seizes and holds back those who are rushing wildly in pursuit of riches and luxury, and, if he does nothing else, at least checks their course—such a man does service to the public though in a private station.
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: When a man withdraws from public life, he should do it in a way that still lets him help others. Whether he's relaxing at home or traveling, he should want to benefit both individuals and all of humanity. He can use his mind, his voice, and his advice. The man who serves the state isn't just the one who nominates candidates, defends people in court, and votes on war and peace. He's also the one who encourages young people to do right. He fills the shortage of good teachers by planting virtue in their minds. He grabs hold of those who are chasing money and luxury like maniacs, and stops them in their tracks — or at least slows them down. This kind of man serves the public even though he holds no office.

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText: Which does the most good, he who decides between foreigners and citizens (as praetor peregrinus), or, as praetor urbanus, pronounces sentence to the suitors in his court at his assistant's dictation, or he who shows them what is meant by justice, filial feeling, endurance, courage, contempt of death and knowledge of the gods, and how much a man is helped by a good conscience? If then you transfer to philosophy the time which you take away from the public service, you will not be a deserter or have refused to perform your proper task.
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: Who does more good? The judge who settles disputes between foreigners and citizens? Or the one who just repeats what his assistant tells him to say in court? Or the person who teaches others what justice really means — what it means to honor your family, endure hardship, show courage, accept death, understand the divine, and know the power of a clear conscience? If you take the time you would have spent in public office and give it to philosophy instead, you're not running away from your duties. You're not refusing to do your proper work.

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText: A soldier is not merely one who stands in the ranks and defends the right or the left wing of the army, but he also who guards the gates—a service which, though less dangerous, is no sinecure—who keeps watch, and takes charge of the arsenal: though all these are bloodless duties, yet they count as military service. As soon as you have devoted yourself to philosophy, you will have overcome all disgust at life: you will not wish for darkness because you are weary of the light, nor will you be a trouble to yourself and useless to others: you will acquire many friends, and all the best men will be attracted towards you: for virtue, in however obscure a position, cannot be hidden, but gives signs of its presence: any one who is worthy will trace it out by its footsteps:
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: A soldier isn't just someone who stands in formation and defends the army's flanks. He's also the one who guards the gates — a job that's less dangerous but still not easy. He keeps watch and manages the weapons. These duties don't involve bloodshed, but they still count as real military service. Once you commit yourself to philosophy, you'll overcome all disgust with life. You won't wish for darkness because you're tired of the light. You won't be a burden to yourself or useless to others. You'll gain many friends, and all the best people will be drawn to you. Virtue can't stay hidden, no matter how humble your position. It always gives signs of itself. Anyone worthy will track it down by following its trail.

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText: but if we give up all society, turn our backs upon the whole human race, and live communing with ourselves alone, this solitude without any interesting occupation will lead to a want of something to do: we shall begin to build up and to pull down, to dam out the sea, to cause waters to flow through natural obstacles, and generally to make a bad disposal of the time which Nature has given us to spend: some of us use it grudgingly, others wastefully; some of us spend it so that we can show a profit and loss account, others so that they have no assets remaining: than which nothing can be more shameful. Often a man who is very old in years has nothing beyond his age by which he can prove that he has lived a long time."
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: But if we give up all social life, turn our backs on the human race, and live alone with just ourselves, this solitude without any meaningful work will leave us with nothing to do. We'll start building things and tearing them down, trying to hold back the sea, forcing water through natural barriers — basically wasting the time that nature gave us to use well. Some of us hoard time like misers. Others throw it away carelessly. Some spend it so they can show what they've accomplished. Others spend it and have nothing left to show for it — which is the most shameful thing of all. Often you'll meet a very old man who has nothing except his age to prove he's been alive for a long time.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText: To me, my dearest Serenus, Athenodorus seems to have yielded too completely to the times, to have fled too soon: I will not deny that sometimes one must retire, but one ought to retire slowly, at a foot's pace, without losing one's ensigns or one's honour as a soldier: those who make terms with arms in their hands are more respected by their enemies and more safe in their hands. This is what I think ought to be done by virtue and by one who practises virtue: if Fortune get the upper hand and deprive him of the power of action, let him not straightway turn his back to the enemy, throw away his arms, and run away seeking for a hiding-place, as if there were any place whither Fortune could not pursue him, but let him be more sparing in his acceptance of public office, and after due deliberation discover some means by which he can be of use to the state.
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish:
My dear Serenus, I think Athenodorus gave up too easily. He ran away too quickly. I won't deny that sometimes you need to step back from public life. But you should retreat slowly, with dignity. Keep your standards and your honor intact. Soldiers who negotiate while still holding their weapons earn more respect from their enemies. They're also safer.

This is what I think virtue should do. This is what anyone practicing virtue should do. If Fortune gets the upper hand and takes away your power to act, don't immediately turn and run. Don't throw down your weapons and scramble for a hiding place. There's nowhere Fortune can't follow you anyway. Instead, be more careful about taking public office. Think it through. Find some way you can still serve the state.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText: He is not able to serve in the army: then let him become a candidate for civic honours: must he live in a private station? then let him be an advocate: is he condemned to keep silence? then let him help his countrymen with silent counsel. Is it dangerous for him even to enter the forum? then let him prove himself a good comrade, a faithful friend, a sober guest in people's houses, at public shows, and at wine-parties. Suppose that he has lost the status of a citizen; then let him exercise that of a man: our reason for magnanimously refusing to confine ourselves within the walls of one city, for having gone forth to enjoy intercourse with all lands and for professing ourselves to be citizens of the world is that we may thus obtain a wider theatre on which to display our virtue.
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish: Can't serve in the army? Then run for public office. Must stay out of politics? Then become a lawyer. Forbidden to speak publicly? Then give quiet advice to your fellow citizens. Too dangerous to even enter the forum? Then be a good friend, a loyal companion, a pleasant guest at dinner parties and public events. Lost your citizenship? Then act like a human being should. We proudly call ourselves citizens of the world, not just one city. We seek contact with all lands. Why? Because it gives us a bigger stage to show our virtue.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText: Is the bench of judges closed to you, are you forbidden to address the people from the hustings, or to be a candidate at elections? then turn your eyes away from Rome, and see what a wide extent of territory, what a number of nations present themselves before you. Thus, it is never possible for so many outlets to be closed against your ambition that more will not remain open to it: but see whether the whole prohibition does not arise from your own fault. You do not choose to direct the affairs of the state except as consul or prytanis or meddix or sufes: what should we say if you refused to serve in the army save as general or military tribune?
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish:
Are you banned from being a judge? Forbidden from speaking to the public or running for office? Then stop looking at Rome and see how big the world is. Look at all the nations out there. It's impossible for every door to your ambitions to be shut — there are always more open. But ask yourself: is this whole ban really someone else's fault, or yours?

You only want to run the government if you can be consul or governor or chief magistrate. What if someone said they'd only serve in the army as a general or top officer?

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText: Even though others may form the first line, and your lot may have placed you among the veterans of the third, do your duty there with your voice, encouragement, example, and spirit: even though a man's hands be cut off, he may find means to help his side in a battle, if he stands his ground and cheers on his comrades. Do something of that sort yourself: if Fortune removes you from the front rank, stand your ground nevertheless and cheer on your comrades, and if somebody stops your mouth, stand nevertheless and help your side in silence.
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish: Even if others are in the front lines and fate has placed you with the older soldiers in back, do your duty there. Use your voice, your encouragement, your example, and your spirit. Even if a man's hands are cut off, he can still help his side in battle if he holds his position and cheers on his comrades. Do something like that yourself. If Fortune pulls you from the front rank, hold your ground anyway and cheer on your comrades. And if someone silences you, still stand firm and help your side quietly.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText: The services of a good citizen are never thrown away: he does good by being heard and seen, by his expression, his gestures, his silent determination, and his very walk. As some remedies benefit us by their smell as well as by their their taste and touch, so virtue even when concealed and at a distance sheds usefulness around. Whether she moves at her ease and enjoys her just rights, or can only appear abroad on sufferance and is forced to shorten sail to the tempest, whether it be unemployed, silent, and pent up in a narrow lodging, or openly displayed, in whatever guise she may appear, she always does good. What? do you think that the example of one who can rest nobly has no value? It is by far the best plan, therefore, to mingle leisure with business, whenever chance impediments or the state of public affairs forbid one's leading an active life: for one is never so cut off from all pursuits as to find no room left for honourable action.
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish:
A good citizen's efforts are never wasted. He helps others just by being heard and seen — through his expression, his gestures, his quiet resolve, and even the way he walks. Some medicines help us through their smell as well as their taste and touch. Virtue works the same way. Even when it's hidden or far away, it spreads usefulness around.

Whether virtue moves freely and enjoys its proper rights, or can only appear in public by permission and must trim its sails against the storm, whether it sits unemployed and silent in cramped quarters, or stands openly displayed — whatever form it takes, it always does good. Do you think there's no value in the example of someone who knows how to rest nobly? 

The best plan is to mix leisure with work whenever obstacles or public affairs prevent you from leading an active life. You're never so cut off from everything that there's no room left for honorable action.

peace-of-mind_section-05.originalText: Could you anywhere find a [more] miserable city than that of Athens when it was being torn to pieces by the thirty tyrants? they slew thirteen hundred citizens, all the best men, and did not leave off because they had done so, but their cruelty became stimulated by exercise. In the city which possessed that most reverend tribunal, the Court of the Areopagus, which possessed a Senate, and a popular assembly which was like a Senate, there met daily a wretched crew of butchers, and the unhappy Senate House was crowded with tyrants. A state, in which there were so many tyrants that they would have been enough to form a bodyguard for one, might surely have rested from the struggle; it seemed impossible for men's minds even to conceive hopes of recovering their liberty, nor could they see any room for a remedy for such a mass of evil: for whence could the unhappy state obtain all the Harmodiuses it would need to slay so many tyrants?
peace-of-mind_section-05.plainEnglish: Could you find a more miserable city than Athens when thirty tyrants were tearing it apart? They killed thirteen hundred citizens — all the best people — and they didn't stop there. The cruelty just made them hungry for more violence. This was the city with the sacred Areopagus court, with a Senate, with a popular assembly that was like another Senate. Now a gang of butchers met there every day. The unhappy Senate House was packed with tyrants. When a state has so many tyrants that they could form one man's bodyguard, you'd think it would give up the fight. It seemed impossible for people to even imagine getting their freedom back. They couldn't see any way out of such a massive evil. Where could this wretched state find enough heroes like Harmodius to kill so many tyrants?

peace-of-mind_section-05.originalText: Yet Socrates was in the midst of the city, and consoled its mourning Fathers, encouraged those who despaired of the republic, by his reproaches brought rich men, who feared that their wealth would be their ruin, to a tardy repentance of their avarice, and moved about as a great example to those who wished to imitate him, because he walked a free man in the midst of thirty masters. However, Athens herself put him to death in prison, and Freedom herself could not endure the freedom of one who had treated a whole band of tyrants with scorn: you may know, therefore, that even in an oppressed state a wise man can find an opportunity for bringing himself to the front, and that in a prosperous and flourishing one wanton insolence, jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly vices bear sway.
peace-of-mind_section-05.plainEnglish: Look at Socrates. He lived right in the middle of the city. He comforted the grieving leaders and gave hope to those who had given up on the republic. He shamed wealthy men who were afraid their riches would destroy them, making them regret their greed. He walked around as a living example for anyone who wanted to follow his lead. He was a free man even though thirty tyrants ruled over everyone else. But Athens still killed him in prison. Even Freedom herself couldn't stand the freedom of a man who had mocked a whole gang of tyrants. This shows you that a wise person can make their mark even in an oppressed state. But in a successful, thriving state, arrogance, jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly vices take control.

peace-of-mind_section-05.originalText: We ought, therefore, to expand or contract ourselves according as the state presents itself to us, or as Fortune offers us opportunities: but in any case we ought to move and not to become frozen still by fear: nay, he is the best man who, though peril menaces him on every side and arms and chains beset his path, nevertheless neither impairs nor conceals his virtue: for to keep oneself safe does not mean to bury oneself. I think that Curius Dentatus spoke truly when he said that he would rather be dead than alive: the worst evil of all is to leave the ranks of the living before one dies: yet it is your duty, if you happen to live in an age when it is not easy to serve the state, to devote more time to leisure and to literature. Thus, just as though you were making a perilous voyage, you may from time to time put into harbour, and set yourself free from public business without waiting for it to do so.
peace-of-mind_section-05.plainEnglish: So we should adjust ourselves based on what the times demand and what Fortune offers us. But either way, we must keep moving — not freeze up from fear. The best person is one who faces danger, weapons, and chains on all sides but still doesn't hide or weaken their virtue. Staying safe doesn't mean burying yourself alive. I think Curius Dentatus was right when he said he'd rather be dead than truly alive. The worst thing of all is to stop living before you actually die. But if you happen to live in times when serving the state is nearly impossible, then it's your duty to spend more time on rest and learning. Think of it like sailing in dangerous waters — sometimes you need to pull into harbor and step away from public life before it forces you out.

peace-of-mind_section-06.originalText: We ought, however, first to examine our own selves, next the business which we propose to transact, next those for whose sake or in whose company we transact it.
peace-of-mind_section-06.plainEnglish: We should first examine ourselves, then the work we plan to do, and finally the people we're doing it for or working with.

peace-of-mind_section-06.originalText: It is above all things necessary to form a true estimate of oneself, because as a rule we think that we can do more than we are able: one man is led too far through confidence in his eloquence, another demands more from his estate than it can produce, another burdens a weakly body with some toilsome duty. Some men are too shamefaced for the conduct of public affairs, which require an unblushing front: some men's obstinate pride renders them unfit for courts: some cannot control their anger, and break into unguarded language on the slightest provocation: some cannot rein in their wit or resist making risky jokes: for all these men leisure is better than employment: a bold, haughty and impatient nature ought to avoid anything that may lead it to use a freedom of speech which will bring it to ruin.
peace-of-mind_section-06.plainEnglish: The most important thing is to know yourself honestly. We usually think we can do more than we actually can. One person gets carried away by his speaking ability. Another expects his money to stretch further than it will. Someone else pushes his weak body to do demanding work. Some people are too shy for politics, which demands a thick skin. Others are too stubborn and proud for court life. Some can't control their temper and say foolish things when slightly annoyed. Others can't hold back their cleverness or stop making dangerous jokes. For all these people, staying out of public life is better than jumping in. If you're bold, arrogant, and impatient, avoid anything that might tempt you to speak too freely — it will destroy you.

peace-of-mind_section-06.originalText: Next we must form an estimate of the matter which we mean to deal with, and compare our strength with the deed we are about to attempt: for the bearer ought always to be more powerful than his load: indeed, loads which are too heavy for their bearer must of necessity crush him: some affairs also are not so important in themselves as they are prolific and lead to much more business, which employments, as they involve us in new and various forms of work, ought to be refused. Neither should you engage in anything from which you are not free to retreat: apply yourself to something which you can finish, or at any rate can hope to finish: you had better not meddle with those operations which grow in importance, while they are being transacted, and which will not stop where you intended them to stop.
peace-of-mind_section-06.plainEnglish: Next, we need to judge what we're taking on. We need to compare our strength with what we're about to attempt. The person carrying the load should always be stronger than the load itself. Loads that are too heavy will crush whoever tries to carry them. Some tasks aren't that big by themselves, but they multiply and lead to much more work. You should refuse these jobs because they drag you into new and different kinds of work. Don't start anything you can't walk away from. Work on something you can finish, or at least hope to finish. It's better to avoid projects that keep growing while you're doing them — projects that won't stop where you planned them to stop.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText: In all cases one should be careful in one's choice of men, and see whether they be worthy of our bestowing a part of our life upon them, or whether we shall waste our own time and theirs also: for some even consider us to be in their debt because of our services to them. Athenodorus said that "he would not so much as dine with a man who would not be grateful to him for doing so": meaning, I imagine, that much less would he go to dinner with those who recompense the services of their friends by their table, and regard courses of dishes as donatives, as if they overate themselves to do honour to others. Take away from these men their witnesses and spectators: they will take no pleasure in solitary gluttony.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: You need to be careful about who you spend time with. Ask yourself: are these people worth giving part of your life to? Or will you just waste your time and theirs? Some people actually think you owe them something when you help them. Athenodorus had a rule: "I wouldn't even have dinner with someone who wouldn't be grateful for my company." What he meant was this: if someone won't appreciate a simple dinner invitation, why would you bother with people who think a fancy meal repays their friends' kindness? These hosts act like serving expensive food is some generous gift, as if stuffing themselves somehow honors their guests. Take away their audience and witnesses — these people have no interest in eating alone.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText: You must decide whether your disposition is better suited for vigorous action or for tranquil speculation and contemplation, and you must adopt whichever the bent of your genius inclines you for. Isocrates laid hands upon Ephorus and led him away from the forum, thinking that he would be more usefully employed in compiling chronicles; for no good is done by forcing one's mind to engage in uncongenial work: it is vain to struggle against Nature.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: You need to figure out what suits you better: active work in the world or quiet thinking and study. Then follow whatever your natural talents pull you toward. Isocrates once grabbed his student Ephorus and dragged him away from public life, thinking he'd be more useful writing history books. There's no point in forcing your mind to do work it's not built for. Fighting against your nature is useless.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText: Yet nothing delights the mind so much as faithful and pleasant friendship: what a blessing it is when there is one whose breast is ready to receive all your secrets with safety, whose knowledge of your actions you fear less than your own conscience, whose conversation removes your anxieties, whose advice assists your plans, whose cheerfulness dispels your gloom, whose very sight delights you!
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: Nothing brings more joy to the mind than a true and pleasant friendship. What a blessing it is to have someone you can tell all your secrets to safely. Someone whose judgment you trust even more than your own conscience. Someone whose conversation eases your worries, whose advice helps your plans, whose good cheer lifts your spirits, and whose very presence makes you happy!

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText: We should choose for our friends men who are, as far as possible, free from strong desires: for vices are contagious, and pass from a man to his neighbour, and injure those who touch them. As, therefore, in times of pestilence we have to be careful not to sit near people who are infected and in whom the disease is raging, because by so doing, we shall run into danger and catch the plague from their very breath; so, too, in choosing our friends' dispositions, we must take care to select those who are as far as may be unspotted by the world; for the way to breed disease is to mix what is sound with what is rotten.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: We should choose friends who are free from strong desires as much as possible. Bad habits spread like a disease. They jump from one person to another and harm anyone who gets close. During a plague, we're careful not to sit near infected people whose disease is raging. We know we'll catch it from their breath if we do. In the same way, when choosing friends, we must pick people who are as clean from worldly corruption as possible. The fastest way to create disease is to mix what's healthy with what's rotten.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText: Yet I do not advise you to follow after or draw to yourself no one except a wise man: for where will you find him whom for so many centuries we have sought in vain? in the place of the best possible man take him who is least bad. You would hardly find any time that would have enabled you to make a happier choice than if you could have sought for a good man from among the Platos and Xenophons and the rest of the produce of the brood of Socrates, or if you had been permitted to choose one from the age of Cato: an age which bore many men worthy to be born in Cato's time (just as it also bore many men worse than were ever known before, planners of the blackest crimes: for it needed both classes in order to make Cato understood: it wanted both good men, that he might win their approbation, and bad men, against whom he could prove his strength): but at the present day, when there is such a dearth of good men, you must be less squeamish in your choice.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: But I'm not telling you to seek out only a wise man as your companion. Where would you find one? We've been looking for centuries and still haven't found him. Instead of the perfect person, choose the least flawed one you can find. You'd be hard-pressed to find a better time for this choice than if you could pick a good man from among Plato, Xenophon, and the other students of Socrates. Or if you could choose someone from Cato's era — a time that produced many men worthy of living alongside Cato. That same age also produced some of the worst men ever known, planners of terrible crimes. Both types were needed to show what Cato truly was. He needed good men to approve of him, and bad men to test his strength against. But today, when good men are so rare, you can't afford to be picky.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText: Above all, however, avoid dismal men who grumble at whatever happens, and find something to complain of in everything. Though he may continue loyal and friendly towards you, still one's peace of mind is destroyed by a comrade whose mind is soured and who meets every incident with a groan.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: Most importantly, stay away from gloomy people who complain about everything that happens. They always find something wrong with every situation. Even if they remain loyal and friendly to you, a companion with a bitter attitude will destroy your peace of mind. They meet every small event with a groan.

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText: Let us now pass on to the consideration of property, that most fertile source of human sorrows: for if you compare all the other ills from which we suffer—deaths, sicknesses, fears, regrets, endurance of pains and labours— with those miseries which our money inflicts upon us, the latter will far outweigh all the others. Reflect, then, how much less a grief it is never to have had any money than to have lost it: we shall thus understand that the less poverty has to lose, the less torment it has with which to afflict us: for you are mistaken if you suppose that the rich bear their losses with greater spirit than the poor: a wound causes the same amount of pain to the greatest and the smallest body.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: Now let's talk about money and possessions — the biggest source of human misery. Compare all our other troubles — death, illness, fear, regret, physical pain and hard work — with the suffering that money causes us. Money troubles will always be worse. Think about this: it hurts much less to never have had money than to lose it. This shows us that the less you have, the less you can lose, and the less you'll suffer. Poor people don't feel financial losses any less than rich people do. You're wrong if you think wealthy people handle losses better. A wound hurts the same whether you're big or small.

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText: It was a neat saying of Bion's, "that it hurts bald men as much as hairy men to have their hairs pulled out": you may be assured that the same thing is true of rich and poor people, that their suffering is equal: for their money clings to both classes, and cannot be torn away without their feeling it: yet it is more endurable, as I have said, and easier not to gain property than to lose it, and therefore you will find that those upon whom Fortune has never smiled are more cheerful than those whom she has deserted.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: Bion had a clever saying: "Pulling out hair hurts just as much whether you're bald or have a full head of hair." You can be sure the same is true for rich and poor people — they suffer equally when they lose money. Money sticks to both types of people and can't be torn away without pain. But as I've said, it's easier to bear not getting something in the first place than losing what you already have. That's why you'll find that people who never had good luck are happier than people who had it and lost it.

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText: Diogenes, a man of infinite spirit, perceived this, and made it impossible that anything should be taken from him. Call this security from loss poverty, want, necessity, or any contemptuous name you please: I shall consider such a man to be happy, unless you find me another who can lose nothing. If I am not mistaken, it is a royal attribute among so many misers, sharpers, and robbers, to be the one man who cannot be injured. If any one doubts the happiness of Diogenes, he would doubt whether the position of the immortal gods was one of sufficient happiness. because they have no farms or gardens, no valuable estates let to strange tenants, and no large loans in the money market.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: Diogenes, a man with enormous spirit, understood this truth. He made it impossible for anyone to take anything away from him. You can call this freedom from loss by any name you want — poverty, want, necessity, or whatever insulting term you prefer. I still think such a man is happy, unless you can show me another person who has nothing to lose. If I'm right, it's a kingly quality in a world full of greedy people, cheaters, and thieves to be the one man who cannot be harmed. Anyone who doubts that Diogenes was happy might as well doubt whether the immortal gods are happy enough — since they don't own farms or gardens, don't have valuable estates rented out to tenants, and don't make big loans in the financial markets.

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText: Are you not ashamed of yourself, you who gaze upon riches with astonished admiration? Look upon the universe: you will see the gods quite bare of property, and possessing nothing though they give everything. Do you think that this man who has stripped himself of all fortuitous accessories is a pauper, or one like to the immortal gods? Do you call Demetrius, Pompeius's freedman, a happier man, he who was not ashamed to be richer than Pompeius, who was daily furnished with a list of the number of his slaves, as a general is with that of his army, though he had long deserved that all his riches should consist of a pair of underlings, and a roomier cell than the other slaves?
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: Aren't you embarrassed? You stare at wealth with wide-eyed wonder. Look at the universe instead. The gods own nothing, yet they give us everything. Do you think a person who has stripped away all these random possessions is poor? Or do you think he's more like the immortal gods? Would you call Demetrius — Pompey's former slave — a happier man? He wasn't ashamed to be richer than his old master. Every day someone brought him a list counting his slaves, like a general getting reports on his army. But he deserved nothing more than two assistants and a prison cell slightly bigger than the other slaves got.

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText: But Diogenes's only slave ran away from him, and when he was pointed out to Diogenes, he did not think him worth fetching back. "It is a shame," he said, "that Manes should be able to live without Diogenes, and that Diogenes should not be able to live without Manes." He seems to me to have said, "Fortune, mind your own business: Diogenes has nothing left that belongs to you. Did my slave run away? nay, he went away from me as a free man."
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: But Diogenes had only one slave, and that slave ran away from him. When someone pointed out where the slave was, Diogenes didn't think he was worth bringing back. "It would be shameful," he said, "if Manes can live without Diogenes, but Diogenes can't live without Manes." To me, it sounds like he was saying, "Fortune, mind your own business! Diogenes has nothing left that you can take from me. Did my slave run away? No — he left me as a free man."

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText: A household of slaves requires food and clothing: the bellies of so many hungry creatures have to be filled: we must buy raiment for them, we must watch their most thievish hands, and we must make use of the services of people who weep and execrate us. How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease! Since we, however, have not such strength of mind as this, we ought at any rate to diminish the extent of our property, in order to be less exposed to the assaults of fortune: those men whose bodies can be within the shelter of their armour, are more fitted for war than those whose huge size everywhere extends beyond it, and exposes them to wounds: the best amount of property to have is that which is enough to keep us from poverty, and which yet is not far removed from it.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: A household full of slaves needs food and clothes. You have to feed all those hungry mouths. You have to buy them clothing and watch their sticky fingers. And you have to rely on people who hate you and curse your name. How much happier is the person who owes nothing to anyone — except for things he can easily give up! But since we don't have that kind of mental strength, we should at least reduce what we own. This makes us less vulnerable to fortune's attacks. In war, soldiers who can fit inside their armor fight better than those whose huge size sticks out everywhere, exposing them to wounds. The best amount of wealth is just enough to keep you out of poverty — but not much more than that.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText: We shall be pleased with this measure of wealth if we have previously taken pleasure in thrift, without which no riches are sufficient, and with which none are insufficient, especially as the remedy is always at hand, and poverty itself by calling in the aid of thrift can convert itself into riches. Let us accustom ourselves to set aside mere outward show, and to measure things by their uses, not by their ornamental trappings: let our hunger be tamed by food, our thirst quenched by drinking, our lust confined within needful bounds; let us learn to use our limbs, and to arrange our dress and way of life according to what was approved of by our ancestors, not in imitation of new-fangled models: let us learn to increase our continence, to repress luxury, to set bounds to our pride, to assuage our anger, to look upon poverty without prejudice, to practise thrift, albeit many are ashamed to do so, to apply cheap remedies to the wants of nature, to keep all undisciplined hopes and aspirations as it were under lock and key, and to make it our business to get our riches from ourselves and not from Fortune.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish:
We'll be happy with whatever wealth we have if we've learned to enjoy living simply. Without this skill, no amount of money is enough. With it, any amount is plenty. The best part is that the solution is always within reach. Even poverty can become wealth if you add some thrift to it.

Let's get used to ignoring flashy displays. Judge things by how useful they are, not by how fancy they look. Use food to satisfy hunger, drink to quench thirst, and keep your desires within reasonable limits. Learn to use your body properly. Dress and live the way our ancestors did — the way that actually worked — instead of chasing every new trend.

Learn to be more self-controlled. Push back against luxury. Put limits on your pride. Cool down your anger. Look at poverty without bias. Practice thrift, even though many people are embarrassed to do it. Use simple, cheap solutions for what your body actually needs. Lock up those wild hopes and dreams that have no discipline behind them. Make it your job to get your riches from yourself, not from luck.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText: We never can so thoroughly defeat the vast diversity and malignity of misfortune with which we are threatened as not to feel the weight of many gusts if we offer a large spread of canvas to the wind: we must draw our affairs into a small compass, to make the darts of Fortune of no avail. For this reason, sometimes slight mishaps have turned into remedies, and more serious disorders have been healed by slighter ones. When the mind pays no attention to good advice, and cannot be brought to its senses by milder measures, why should we not think that its interests are being served by poverty, disgrace, or financial ruin being applied to it? one evil is balanced by another.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish: We can never fully protect ourselves from all the bad luck that threatens us. If we spread ourselves too thin, we'll feel the impact of every storm. We need to keep our lives simple and focused, so Fortune's arrows can't find their mark. Sometimes small setbacks actually help us. And serious problems are often cured by lighter ones. When your mind won't listen to good advice and gentler methods don't work, why not consider that poverty, disgrace, or financial ruin might actually be serving your best interests? Sometimes one trouble cancels out another.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText: Let us then teach ourselves to be able to dine without all Rome to look on, to be the slaves of fewer slaves, to get clothes which fulfil their original purpose, and to live in a smaller house. The inner curve is the one to take, not only in running races and in the contests of the circus, but also in the race of life; even literary pursuits, the most becoming thing for a gentleman to spend money upon, are only justifiable as long as they are kept within bounds.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish: Let's learn to eat dinner without needing all of Rome to watch us. Let's have fewer servants bossing us around. Let's buy clothes that actually serve their purpose. Let's live in smaller houses. In chariot races, the smart driver takes the inside track. The same goes for life itself. Even books and learning — the most respectable way for a gentleman to spend money — only make sense if you don't go overboard.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText: What is the use of possessing numberless books and libraries, whose titles their owner can hardly read through in a lifetime? A student is overwhelmed by such a mass, not instructed, and it is much better to devote yourself to a few writers than to skim through many. Forty thousand books were burned at Alexandria: some would have praised this library as a most noble memorial of royal wealth, like Titus Livius, who says that it was "a splendid result of the taste and attentive care of the kings." It had nothing to do with taste or care, but was a piece of learned luxury, nay, not even learned, since they amassed it, not for the sake of learning, but to make a show, like many men who know less about letters than a slave is expected to know, and who uses his books not to help him in his studies but to ornament his dining-room.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish: What's the point of owning countless books and libraries when you can barely read through all the titles in a lifetime? A student gets overwhelmed by such a huge collection instead of learning from it. It's much better to focus on a few good writers than to skim through many. Forty thousand books burned at Alexandria. Some people praised this library as a wonderful monument to royal wealth, like Titus Livius, who called it "a splendid result of the kings' taste and careful attention." But it had nothing to do with taste or care. It was just scholarly showing off — not even scholarly, really, since they collected books not to learn but to impress people. Many men know less about literature than we'd expect from a slave, yet they use their books not for study but as dining room decorations.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText: Let a man, then, obtain as many books as he wants, but none for show. "It is more respectable," say you, "to spend one's money on such books than on vases of Corinthian brass and paintings." Not so: everything that is carried to excess is wrong. What excuses can you find for a man who is eager to buy bookcases of ivory and citrus wood, to collect the works of unknown or discredited authors, and who sits yawning amid so many thousands of books, whose backs and titles please him more than any other part of them? Thus in the houses of the laziest of men you will see the works of all the orators and historians stacked upon book-shelves reaching right up to the ceiling. At the present day a library has become as necessary an appendage to a house as a hot and cold bath. I would excuse them straightway if they really were carried away by an excessive zeal for literature; but as it is, these costly works of sacred genius, with all the illustrations that adorn them, are merely bought for display and to serve as wall-furniture.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish: Get as many books as you want, but don't buy them just to show off. "It's better," you say, "to spend money on books than on fancy bronze vases and paintings." Not really. Anything taken to excess is wrong. What's your excuse for someone who buys ivory and exotic wood bookcases, collects works by unknown or terrible authors, and sits yawning among thousands of books? He likes their spines and titles more than what's actually inside them. You'll find this in the homes of the laziest people — shelves packed floor to ceiling with works by every famous speaker and historian. These days a library has become as essential to a house as hot and cold running water. I'd forgive them if they were really obsessed with reading. But they're not. These expensive works of brilliant minds, with all their beautiful illustrations, are just bought for show — fancy wall decorations.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText: Suppose, however, that your life has become full of trouble, and that without knowing what you were doing you have fallen into some snare which either public or private Fortune has set for you, and that you can neither untie it nor break it: then remember that fettered men suffer much at first from the burdens and clogs upon their legs: afterwards, when they have made up their minds not to fret themselves about them, but to endure them, necessity teaches them to bear them bravely, and habit to bear them easily. In every station of life you will find amusements, relaxations, and enjoyments; that is, provided you be willing to make light of evils rather than to hate them.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: But suppose your life has become full of trouble. You didn't see it coming, but you've fallen into a trap that either public or private fortune set for you. You can't untie it or break free. Remember this: prisoners suffer terribly at first from the chains around their legs. But once they stop fighting the chains and accept them, necessity teaches them to bear the weight with courage. Habit makes it easier. In every situation in life, you'll find ways to enjoy yourself, to relax, to find pleasure — as long as you're willing to make light of your troubles instead of hating them.
