peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText: Knowing to what sorrows we were born, there is nothing for which Nature more deserves our thanks than for having invented habit as an alleviation of misfortune, which soon accustoms us to the severest evils. No one could hold out against misfortune if it permanently exercised the same force as at its first onset. We are all chained to Fortune: some men's chain is loose and made of gold, that of others is tight and of meaner metal: but what difference does this make? we are all included in the same captivity, and even those who have bound us are bound themselves, unless you think that a chain on the left side is lighter to bear: one man may be bound by public office, another by wealth: some have to bear the weight of illustrious, some of humble birth: some are subject to the commands of others, some only to their own: some are kept in one place by being banished thither, others by being elected to the priesthood. All life is slavery: let each man therefore reconcile himself to his lot, complain of it as little as possible, and lay hold of whatever good lies within his reach.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: Since we know what sorrows we're born into, we should thank Nature for nothing more than giving us habit. Habit softens misfortune and helps us get used to even the worst troubles. No one could survive misfortune if it kept hitting us with the same force it has when it first strikes. We are all chained to Fortune. Some people's chains are loose and made of gold. Others have tight chains made of cheaper metal. But what difference does it make? We're all prisoners together. Even the people who chained us are chained themselves — unless you think a chain on your left side weighs less than one on your right. One person might be bound by public office, another by wealth. Some carry the burden of famous birth, others of humble birth. Some must obey other people's commands, others only their own. Some are stuck in one place because they were banished there, others because they were chosen for the priesthood. All life is slavery. So each person should accept their situation, complain as little as possible, and grab whatever good they can find.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText: No condition can be so wretched that an impartial mind can find no compensations in it. Small sites, if ingeniously divided, may be made use of for many different purposes, and arrangement will render ever so narrow a room habitable. Call good sense to your aid against difficulties: it is possible to soften what is harsh, to widen what is too narrow, and to make heavy burdens press less severely upon one who bears them skilfully.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: No situation is so terrible that a fair mind can't find some good in it. Even tiny spaces can serve many purposes if you arrange them cleverly. Good planning can make even the smallest room livable. Use your common sense when facing problems. You can soften what feels harsh, expand what feels cramped, and make heavy loads feel lighter when you carry them with skill.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText: Moreover, we ought not to allow our desires to wander far afield, but we must make them confine themselves to our immediate neighbourhood, since they will not endure to be altogether locked up. We must leave alone things which either cannot come to pass or can only be effected with difficulty, and follow after such things as are near at hand and within reach of our hopes, always remembering that all things are equally unimportant, and that though they have a different outward appearance, they are all alike empty within.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: We shouldn't let our desires chase after distant things. Instead, we should focus them on what's nearby and achievable. Our desires won't tolerate being completely shut down. We must avoid things that either can't happen or would be extremely hard to get. Instead, we should pursue what's close at hand and within reach. Always remember that all things are equally unimportant. They may look different on the outside, but inside they're all equally empty.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText: Neither let us envy those who are in high places: the heights which look lofty to us are steep and rugged. Again, those whom unkind fate has placed in critical situations will be safer if they show as little pride in their proud position as may be, and do all they are able to bring down their fortunes to the level of other men's. There are many who must needs cling to their high pinnacle of power, because they cannot descend from it save by falling headlong: yet they assure us that their greatest burden is being obliged to be burdensome to others, and that they are nailed to their lofty post rather than raised to it: let them then, by dispensing justice, clemency, and kindness with an open and liberal hand, provide themselves with assistance to break their fall, and looking forward to this maintain their position more hopefully.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: Don't envy those in high positions. What looks impressive from down here is actually steep and dangerous. When cruel fate puts people in risky situations, they'll be safer if they show less pride in their status. They should do everything they can to bring their fortunes down to everyone else's level. Many people have to cling to their high positions because they can't step down without falling hard. They tell us their worst burden is having to burden others. They say they're nailed to their high post rather than lifted up to it. So let them help themselves by freely giving out justice, mercy, and kindness. This will give them something to cushion their fall. Looking ahead to this possibility, they can hold their position with more hope.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText: Yet nothing sets us free from these alternations of hope and fear so well as always fixing some limit to our successes, and not allowing Fortune to choose when to stop our career, but to halt of our own accord long before we apparently need do so. By acting thus certain desires will rouse up our spirits, and yet being confined within bounds, will not lead us to embark on vast and vague enterprises.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: Nothing frees us from swinging between hope and fear like setting our own limits on success. Don't let Fortune decide when to stop your career — stop on your own terms, well before you think you need to. This way, you'll still have desires that motivate you. But they'll stay within bounds and won't drag you into huge, vague projects.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: These remarks of mine apply only to imperfect, commonplace, and unsound natures, not to the wise man, who needs not to walk with timid and cautious gait: for he has such confidence in himself that he does not hesitate to go directly in the teeth of Fortune, and never will give way to her. Nor indeed has he any reason for fearing her, for he counts not only chattels, property, and high office, but even his body, his eyes, his hands, and everything whose use makes life dearer to us, nay, even his very self, to be things whose possession is uncertain; he lives as though he had borrowed them, and is ready to return them cheerfully whenever they are claimed.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: What I've said only applies to imperfect, ordinary people with weak character — not to the wise person. The wise person doesn't need to walk carefully or timidly through life. He has such confidence in himself that he goes straight at Fortune without hesitation. He'll never back down from her. And he has no reason to fear her either. He doesn't just count his money, property, and job as uncertain — he counts his body, his eyes, his hands, and everything that makes life precious to him as uncertain too. Even his very self. He lives as if he had borrowed all these things, and he's ready to give them back cheerfully whenever they're asked for.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: Yet he does not hold himself cheap, because he knows that he is not his own, but performs all his duties as carefully and prudently as a pious and scrupulous man would take care of property left in his charge as trustee. When he is bidden to give them up, he will not complain of Fortune, but will say, "I thank you for what I have had possession of: I have managed your property so as largely to increase it, but since you order me, I give it back to you and return it willingly and thankfully. If you still wish me to own anything of yours, I will keep it for you: if you have other views, I restore into your hands and make restitution of all my wrought and coined silver, my house and my household. Should Nature recall what she previously entrusted us with, let us say to her also: 'Take back my spirit, which is better than when you gave it me: I do not shuffle or hang back. Of my own free will I am ready to return what you gave me before I could think: take me away,'"
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: Yet he doesn't think little of himself, because he knows he doesn't own himself. He performs all his duties carefully and wisely, like a trustworthy person managing someone else's property. When he's told to give these things up, he won't complain to Fortune. Instead he'll say, "Thank you for what I've been allowed to use. I've managed your property well and made it grow. But since you're asking for it back, I return it willingly and gratefully. If you still want me to keep anything of yours, I'll take care of it. If not, I give back everything — my silver, my house, my household." If Nature wants back what she first gave us, let's say to her too: "Take back my spirit, which is better than when you gave it to me. I'm not stalling or holding back. I'm ready to return what you gave me before I could even think. Take me away."

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: What hardship can there be in returning to the place from whence one came? a man cannot live well if he knows not how to die well. We must, therefore, take away from this commodity its original value, and count the breath of life as a cheap matter. "We dislike gladiators," says Cicero, "if they are eager to save their lives by any means whatever: but we look favourably upon them if they are openly reckless of them," You may be sure that the same thing occurs with us: we often die because we are afraid of death. Fortune, which regards our lives as a show in the arena for her own enjoyment, says, "Why should I spare you, base and cowardly creature that you are? you will be pierced and hacked with all the more wounds because you know not how to offer your throat to the knife: whereas you, who receive the stroke without drawing away your neck or putting up your hands to stop it, shall both live longer and die more quickly,"
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: What's so hard about going back to where you came from? A person cannot live well if they don't know how to die well. So we need to stop treating life like it's precious. We should think of our breath as something cheap. Cicero said, "We hate gladiators who desperately try to save their lives by any means. But we admire those who openly don't care if they die." You can be sure the same thing happens with us. We often die because we're afraid of death. Fortune treats our lives like a show in the arena for her entertainment. She says, "Why should I spare you, coward? You'll get cut up with even more wounds because you don't know how to offer your throat to the blade. But you who take the blow without pulling back your neck or raising your hands to block it — you'll live longer and die more quickly."

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: He who fears death will never act as becomes a living man: but he who knows that this fate was laid upon him as soon as he was conceived will live according to it, and by this strength of mind will gain this further advantage, that nothing can befal him unexpectedly: for by looking forward to everything which can happen as though it would happen to him, he takes the sting out of all evils, which can make no difference to those who expect it and are prepared to meet it: evil only comes hard upon those who have lived without giving it a thought and whose attention has been exclusively directed to happiness.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: If you fear death, you'll never truly live. But if you accept that death was your fate from the moment you were born, you'll live according to that truth. This mindset gives you another benefit: nothing will catch you off guard. When you expect that anything bad could happen to you, you take away the power of misfortune. Bad things can't hurt people who see them coming and are ready for them. Trouble only hits hard when it surprises people who never thought about it — people who only focused on being happy.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: Disease, captivity, disaster, conflagration, are none of them unexpected: I always knew with what disorderly company Nature had associated me. The dead have often been wailed for in my neighbourhood: the torch and taper have often been borne past my door before the bier of one who has died before his time: the crash of falling buildings has often resounded by my side: night has snatched away many of those with whom I have become intimate in the forum, the Senate-house, and in society, and has sundered the hands which were joined in friendship: ought I to be surprised if the dangers which have always been circling around me at last assail me? How large a part of mankind never think of storms when about to set sail?
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: Disease, imprisonment, disaster, fires — none of these should surprise us. I've always known what chaotic company Nature has given me as fellow humans. People have died in my neighborhood many times. I've often seen funeral torches carried past my door for someone who died too young. Buildings have collapsed near me. Night has taken away many people I knew from the forum, the Senate, and social life. It has broken apart hands that were joined in friendship. Should I really be surprised when dangers that have always circled around me finally strike? How many people never think about storms when they're about to sail?

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: I shall never be ashamed to quote a good saying because it comes from a bad author. Publilius, who was a more powerful writer than any of our other playwrights, whether comic or tragic, whenever he chose to rise above farcical absurdities and speeches addressed to the gallery, among many other verses too noble even for tragedy, let alone for comedy, has this one:— "What one hath suffered may befall us all." If a man takes this into his inmost heart and looks upon all the misfortunes of other men, of which there is always a great plenty, in this spirit, remembering that there is nothing to prevent their coming upon him also, he will arm himself against them long before they attack him. It is too late to school the mind to endurance of peril after peril has come.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: I'll never be embarrassed to quote something good just because it comes from a bad person. Publilius was better than any of our other playwrights, whether they wrote comedies or tragedies. When he stopped writing cheap laughs and crowd-pleasers, he produced some truly noble lines — too good even for serious drama. One of them goes: "What happened to one person can happen to us all." If you really take this to heart and look at other people's troubles (and there are always plenty), remembering that nothing stops the same things from happening to you, you'll prepare yourself long before disaster strikes. It's too late to train your mind for danger after the danger has already arrived.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: "I did not think this would happen," and "Would you ever have believed that this would have happened?" say you. But why should it not? Where are the riches after which want, hunger, and beggary do not follow? what office is there whose purple robe, augur's staff, and patrician reins have not as their accompaniment rags and banishment, the brand of infamy, a thousand disgraces, and utter reprobation? what kingdom is there for which ruin, trampling under foot, a tyrant and a butcher are not ready at hand? nor are these matters divided by long periods of time, but there is but the space of an hour between sitting on the throne ourselves and clasping the knees of some one else as suppliants. Know then that every station of life is transitory, and that what has ever happened to anybody may happen to you also.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: You say, "I never thought this would happen," and "Who could have believed this would happen?" But why shouldn't it happen? Show me any fortune that isn't followed by poverty, hunger, and want. Show me any high office where the purple robes, ceremonial staff, and noble privileges don't come with the risk of rags, exile, public shame, and complete disgrace. Show me any kingdom that doesn't have ruin, defeat, and a tyrant with a sword waiting in the wings. These changes don't take years to happen — there's often just an hour between sitting on a throne and begging on your knees. So understand this: every position in life is temporary. Whatever has happened to anyone else can happen to you too.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: You are wealthy: are you wealthier than Pompeius? Yet when Gaius, his old relative and new host, opened Caesar's house to him in order that he might close his own, he lacked both bread and water: though he owned so many rivers which both rose and discharged themselves within his dominions, yet he had to beg for drops of water: he perished of hunger and thirst in the palace of his relative, while his heir was contracting for a public funeral for one who was in want of food. You have filled public offices: were they either as important, as unlooked for, or as all-embracing as those of Sejanus? Yet on the day on which the Senate disgraced him, the people tore him to pieces: the executioner could find no part left large enough to drag to the Tiber, of one upon whom gods and men had showered all that could be given to man.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: You are wealthy: are you wealthier than Pompey? Yet when Gaius, his old relative and new host, opened Caesar's house to him so that he might close his own, he lacked both bread and water. Though he owned so many rivers that both began and ended within his territories, he had to beg for drops of water. He died of hunger and thirst in his relative's palace, while his heir was arranging a public funeral for someone who was starving. You have held public offices: were they as important, as unexpected, or as comprehensive as those of Sejanus? Yet on the day the Senate disgraced him, the people tore him to pieces. The executioner could find no part left large enough to drag to the Tiber — this man on whom gods and men had showered everything that could be given to a human being.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: You are a king: I will not bid you go to Croesus for an example, he who while yet alive saw his funeral pile both lighted and extinguished, being made to outlive not only his kingdom but even his own death, nor to Jugurtha, whom the people of Rome beheld as a captive within the year in which they had feared him. We have seen Ptolemaeus King of Africa, and Mithridates King of Armenia, under the charge of Gaius's guards: the former was sent into exile, the latter chose it in order to make his exile more honourable. Among such continual topsy-turvy changes, unless you expect that whatever can happen will happen to you, you give adversity power against you, a power which can be destroyed by any one who looks at it beforehand.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: You are a king: I won't tell you to look at Croesus as an example. He watched his own funeral pyre being lit and put out while he was still alive. He lived to see not just his kingdom fall, but his own death rehearsed. I won't mention Jugurtha either — the Romans captured him within a year of fearing him. We've seen Ptolemy, King of Africa, and Mithridates, King of Armenia, both under guard by Gaius's soldiers. One was sent into exile, the other chose exile to make it more honorable. With such constant upheavals happening everywhere, you give misfortune power over you unless you expect that whatever can happen will happen to you. Anyone who thinks about this beforehand can destroy that power.

peace-of-mind_section-12.originalText: The next point to these will be to take care that we do not labour for what is vain, or labour in vain: that is to say, neither to desire what we are not able to obtain, nor yet, having obtained our desire too late, and after much toil to discover the folly of our wishes: in other words, that our labour may not be without result, and that the result may not be unworthy of our labour: for as a rule sadness arises from one of these two things, either from want of success or from being ashamed of having succeeded.
peace-of-mind_section-12.plainEnglish: The next step is to make sure we don't work for pointless things or work pointlessly. This means two things: don't chase what you can't actually get, and don't spend years struggling for something only to realize too late that you never really wanted it. In other words, make sure your work actually leads somewhere, and make sure that somewhere is worth going. Most sadness comes from one of these two mistakes: either failing to get what you wanted, or getting it and then feeling embarrassed about having wanted it in the first place.

peace-of-mind_section-12.originalText: We must limit the running to and fro which most men practise, rambling about houses, theatres, and market-places. They mind other men's business, and always seem as though they themselves had something to do. If you ask one of them as he comes out of his own door, "Whither are you going?" he will answer, "By Hercules, I do not know: but I shall see some people and do something." They wander purposelessly seeking for something to do, and do, not what they have made up their minds to do, but what has casually fallen in their way. They move uselessly and without any plan, just like ants crawling over bushes, which creep up to the top and then down to the bottom again without gaining anything. Many men spend their lives in exactly the same fashion, which one may call a state of restless indolence.
peace-of-mind_section-12.plainEnglish: We need to stop all this running around that most people do. They wander aimlessly from house to house, from theaters to markets. They stick their noses into other people's business and always act like they have something important to do. Ask someone as they leave their house, "Where are you going?" They'll say, "I honestly don't know, but I'll see some people and do something." They drift around looking for something to do. But they don't do what they planned — they just do whatever happens to cross their path. They move around pointlessly, with no real plan. They're like ants crawling over bushes, climbing up to the top and then back down to the bottom, getting nowhere. Many people live their whole lives this way. You could call it restless laziness.

peace-of-mind_section-12.originalText: You would pity some of them when you see them running as if their house was on fire: they actually jostle all whom they meet, and hurry along themselves and others with them, though all the while they are going to salute some one who will not return their greeting, or to attend the funeral of some one whom they did not know: they are going to hear the verdict on one who often goes to law, or to see the wedding of one who often gets married: they will follow a man's litter, and in some places will even carry it: afterwards returning home weary with idleness, they swear that they themselves do not know why they went out, or where they have been, and on the following day they will wander through the same round again.
peace-of-mind_section-12.plainEnglish: You would feel sorry for some of these people when you see them running around like their house is on fire. They bump into everyone they meet and rush themselves and others along with them. But where are they going? To greet someone who won't greet them back. To attend a funeral for someone they didn't even know. To hear the verdict for someone who's always in court. To watch a wedding for someone who gets married all the time. They'll follow some important person's sedan chair, and in some places they'll even help carry it. Then they come home exhausted from all this meaningless activity. They swear they don't even know why they went out or where they've been. And the next day? They'll do the exact same thing all over again.

peace-of-mind_section-12.originalText: Let all your work, therefore, have some purpose, and keep some object in view: these restless people are not made restless by labour, but are driven out of their minds by mistaken ideas: for even they do not put themselves in motion without any hope: they are excited by the outward appearance of something, and their crazy mind cannot see its futility. In the same way every one of those who walk out to swell the crowd in the streets, is led round the city by worthless and empty reasons; the dawn drives him forth, although he has nothing to do, and after he has pushed his way into many men's doors, and saluted their nomenclators one after the other, and been turned away from many others, he finds that the most difficult person of all to find at home is himself. From this evil habit comes that worst of all vices, talebearing and prying into public and private secrets, and the knowledge of many things which it is neither safe to tell nor safe to listen to.
peace-of-mind_section-12.plainEnglish: So make sure all your work has a real purpose. Keep some clear goal in mind. Restless people aren't driven by hard work — they're driven crazy by confused thinking. Even they don't move around without some hope. They get excited by how things look on the surface. Their mixed-up minds can't see how pointless it all is. It's the same with everyone who goes out to join the crowds in the streets. They get led around the city by worthless, empty reasons. Dawn pushes them out the door even when they have nothing to do. They push their way to many people's doors. They greet doorkeeper after doorkeeper. They get turned away from many houses. And they discover that the hardest person to find at home is themselves. This bad habit leads to the worst vice of all: gossiping and prying into public and private secrets. They learn many things that are dangerous both to tell and to hear.

peace-of-mind_section-13.originalText:
It was, I imagine, following out this principle that Democritis
taught that “he who would live at peace must not do much business
either public or private,” referring of course to unnecessary
business: for if there be any necessity for it we ought to transact
not only much but endless business, both public and private; in
cases, however, where no solemn duty invites us to act, we had
better keep ourselves quiet: for he who does many things often puts
himself in Fortune’s power, and it is safest not to tempt her often,
but always to remember her existence, and never to promise oneself
anything on her security.
peace-of-mind_section-13.plainEnglish: I think this is what Democritus meant when he said, "Anyone who wants to live peacefully shouldn't do too much business, whether public or private." He was talking about unnecessary business, of course. When duty calls, we should handle not just a lot of business, but endless amounts — both public and private. But when no serious obligation requires us to act, we're better off staying quiet. The person who does many things often puts himself at Fortune's mercy. It's safest not to tempt her too often. Always remember she exists, and never promise yourself anything based on her favor.

peace-of-mind_section-13.originalText:
I will set sail unless anything happens
to prevent me, I shall be praetor, if nothing hinders me, my
financial operations will succeed, unless anything goes wrong with
them. This is why we say that nothing befals the wise man which he
did not expect—we do not make him exempt from the chances of human
life, but from its mistakes, nor does everything happen to him as
he wished it would, but as he thought it would: now his first thought
was that his purpose might meet with some resistance, and the pain
of disappointed wishes must affect a man’s mind less severely if
he has not been at all events confident of success.
peace-of-mind_section-13.plainEnglish: I will set sail unless something stops me. I'll become praetor if nothing gets in my way. My business deals will work out unless something goes wrong. This is why we say nothing happens to a wise person that they didn't expect. We don't make them immune to life's random events, but we do protect them from life's mistakes. Not everything happens as they wished, but it happens as they thought it would. Their first thought was always that their plans might hit some resistance. The pain of failed hopes hurts much less when you weren't completely confident of success in the first place.

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Moreover, we ought to cultivate an easy temper, and not become over fond of the lot which fate has assigned to us, but transfer ourselves to whatever other condition chance may lead us to, and fear no alteration, either in our purposes or our position in life, provided that we do not become subject to caprice, which of all vices is the most hostile to repose: for obstinacy, from which Fortune often wrings some concession, must needs be anxious and unhappy, but caprice, which can never restrain itself, must be more so. Both of these qualities, both that of altering nothing, and that of being dissatisfied with everything, are energies to repose.
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: We should also develop an easy-going temperament. Don't get too attached to whatever life fate has given you. Be ready to adapt when circumstances push you toward something new. Don't fear changes in your goals or your position in life — just avoid being fickle. Of all character flaws, fickleness is the most destructive to peace of mind. Stubbornness makes you anxious and miserable (though Fortune sometimes forces stubborn people to give in). But fickleness is even worse because it never lets you rest. Both extremes — never changing anything and being dissatisfied with everything — are enemies of inner peace.

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: The mind ought in all cases to be called away from the contemplation of external things to that of itself: let it confide in itself, rejoice in itself, admire its own works; avoid as far as may be those of others, and devote itself to itself; let it not feel losses, and put a good construction even upon misfortunes. Zeno, the chief of our school, when he heard the news of a shipwreck, in which all his property had been lost, remarked, "Fortune bids me follow philosophy in lighter marching order."
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Your mind should always turn away from focusing on outside things and look inward instead. Let it trust itself, find joy in itself, and admire its own achievements. Avoid other people's business as much as possible, and focus on yourself. Don't feel crushed by losses. Try to see even bad luck in a positive light. Zeno, the founder of our philosophy, heard that a shipwreck had destroyed all his property. His response? "Fortune is telling me to pursue philosophy with less baggage."

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death, and even with want of burial. "You are able to please yourself," he answered, "my half pint of blood is in your power: for, as for burial, what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it."
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: A tyrant threatened to kill Theodorus and leave his body unburied. Theodorus replied, "Do whatever makes you happy. You can spill my blood if you want — that's up to you. But as for burial, you'd have to be an idiot to think I care whether I rot above ground or underground."

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Julius Kanus, a man of peculiar greatness, whom even the fact of his having been born in this century does not prevent our admiring, had a long dispute with Gaius, and when as he was going away that Phalaris of a man said to him, "That you may not delude yourself with any foolish hopes, I have ordered you to be executed," he answered, "I thank you, most excellent prince." I am not sure what he meant: for many ways of explaining his conduct occur to me. Did he wish to be reproachful, and to show him how great his cruelty must be if death became a kindness? or did he upbraid him with his accustomed insanity? for even those whose children were put to death, and whose goods were confiscated, used to thank him: or was it that he willingly received death, regarding it as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a magnanimous answer.
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Julius Kanus was a man of extraordinary greatness. Even the fact that he lived in our terrible times doesn't stop us from admiring him. He had a long argument with Gaius. As he was leaving, that tyrant said to him, "Don't fool yourself with false hope. I've ordered you to be executed." Kanus replied, "Thank you, most excellent prince." I'm not sure what he meant. Several explanations come to mind. Was he being sarcastic to show Gaius how cruel he was — that death had become a mercy? Was he mocking the emperor's well-known madness? Even people whose children were killed and property seized used to thank Gaius. Or did Kanus welcome death because he saw it as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a brave answer.

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Some one may say, "After this Gaius might have let him live." Kanus had no fear of this: the good faith with which Gaius carried out such orders as these was well known. Will you believe that he passed the ten intervening days before his execution without the slightest despondency? it is marvellous how that man spoke and acted, and how peaceful he was. He was playing at draughts when the centurion in charge of a number of those who where going to be executed bade him join them: on the summons he counted his men and said to his companion, "Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won;" then, turning to the centurion, he said "You will bear me witness that I am one man ahead of him." Do you think that Kanus played upon that draught-board? nay, he played with it.
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Someone might say, "After this, Gaius could have let him live." But Kanus wasn't worried about that. Everyone knew how reliably Gaius followed through on execution orders. Can you believe that Kanus spent the ten days before his death without any despair? It's amazing how calmly he spoke and acted. How peaceful he was. He was playing checkers when the centurion came to collect the condemned prisoners. When called, Kanus counted his pieces and said to his opponent, "Don't lie after I'm dead and claim you were winning." Then he turned to the centurion and said, "You can witness that I'm ahead by one piece." Do you think Kanus was just playing a game on that board? No — he was playing with death itself.

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life, which used its own fate as a proof of truth, which when at the last step of life experimented upon his fleeting breath, and did not merely continue to learn until he died, but learned something even from death itself. No man has carried the life of a philosopher further. I will not hastily leave the subject of a great man, and one who deserves to be spoken of with respect: I will hand thee down to all posterity, thou most noble heart, chief among the many victims of Gaius.
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Here was peace in the middle of chaos. Here was a soul that deserved to live forever — one who used his own suffering as proof of what he believed. Even at death's door, he kept experimenting with his last breaths. He didn't just keep learning until he died. He learned something from death itself. No one has lived the philosopher's life more completely. I won't quickly move on from talking about such a great man — one who deserves our respect. I will pass your memory down to future generations, you most noble heart, greatest among all the many victims of Gaius.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: Yet we gain nothing by getting rid of all personal causes of sadness, for sometimes we are possessed by hatred of the human race. When you reflect how rare simplicity is, how unknown innocence, how seldom faith is kept, unless it be to our advantage, when you remember such numbers of successful crimes, so many equally hateful losses and gains of lust, and ambition so impatient even of its own natural limits that it is willing to purchase distinction by baseness, the mind seems as it were cast into darkness, and shadows rise before it as though the virtues were all overthrown and we were no longer allowed to hope to possess them or benefited by their possession.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: But even when we fix our personal problems, we still feel sad sometimes. That's because we start to hate humanity itself. Think about how rare honest people are. How few innocent people you meet. How seldom people keep their word unless it benefits them. Remember all the crimes that go unpunished. All the disgusting ways people chase money and power. Think about ambition so desperate that people will do shameful things just to stand out. When you see all this, your mind goes dark. It feels like virtue has been completely destroyed. You start to think there's no point in being good, and that good people get nothing for their efforts.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: We ought therefore to bring ourselves into such a state of mind that all the vices of the vulgar may not appear hateful to us, but merely ridiculous, and we should imitate Democritus rather than Heraclitus. The latter of these, whenever be appeared in public, used to weep, the former to laugh: the one thought all human doings to be follies, the other thought them to be miseries. We must take a higher view of all things, and bear with them more easily: it better becomes a man to scoff at life than to lament over it.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: We should train our minds to see the common faults of people as funny rather than hateful. We should be like Democritus, not Heraclitus. Heraclitus would cry whenever he went out in public. Democritus would laugh. One saw human behavior as tragic. The other saw it as foolish. We need to take a bigger view of everything and put up with it more easily. It's better for a person to laugh at life than to cry over it.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: Add to this that he who laughs at the human race deserves better of it than he who mourns for it, for the former leaves it some good hopes of improvement, while the latter stupidly weeps over what he has given up all hopes of mending. He who after surveying the universe cannot control his laughter shows, too, a greater mind than he who cannot restrain his tears, because his mind is only affected in the slightest possible degree, and he does not think that any part of all this apparatus is either important, or serious, or unhappy.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: There's another point worth making. Someone who laughs at the human race treats it better than someone who mourns for it. The one who laughs still has hope that things can get better. The one who mourns has foolishly given up — he's crying over something he thinks can't be fixed. When someone looks at the whole universe and can't help but laugh, he shows a bigger mind than someone who can't stop his tears. His mind is barely affected by any of it. He doesn't think any part of this whole show is important, serious, or tragic.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: As for the several causes which render us happy or sorrowful, let every one describe them for himself, and learn the truth of Bion's saying, "That all the doings of men were very like what he began with, and that there is nothing in their lives which is more holy or decent than their conception." Yet it is better to accept public morals and human vices calmly without bursting into either laughter or tears; for to be hurt by the sufferings of others is to be for ever miserable, while to enjoy the sufferings of others is an inhuman pleasure, just as it is a useless piece of humanity to weep and pull a long face because some one is burying his son.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: Everyone should look at what makes them happy or sad and decide for themselves. They'll learn the truth of what Bion said: "All human behavior is just like how we started out. There's nothing in our lives that's more pure or decent than our birth." But it's better to accept society's flaws and human vices with calm. Don't burst into laughter or tears over them. If you let other people's suffering hurt you, you'll be miserable forever. But if you enjoy other people's suffering, that's cruel. And it's pointless to cry and look sad just because someone is burying their child.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: In one's own misfortunes, also, one ought so to conduct oneself as to bestow upon them just as much sorrow as reason, not as much as custom requires: for many shed tears in order to show them, and whenever no one is looking at them their eyes are dry, but they think it disgraceful not to weep when every one does so. So deeply has this evil of being guided by the opinion of others taken root in us, that even grief, the simplest of all emotions, begins to be counterfeited.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: When bad things happen to you, you should feel only as much sadness as makes sense — not as much as everyone expects you to feel. Many people cry just for show. When no one is watching, their eyes are dry. But they think it would be shameful not to weep when everyone else does. This disease of living by other people's opinions has infected us so deeply that even grief — the most natural emotion of all — becomes fake.

peace-of-mind_section-16.originalText: There comes now a part of our subject which is wont with good cause to make one sad and anxious: I mean when good men come to bad ends; when Socrates is forced to die in prison, Rutilius to live in exile, Pompeius and Cicero to offer their necks to the swords of their own followers, when the great Cato, that living image of virtue, falls upon his sword and rips up both himself and the republic, one cannot help being grieved that Fortune should bestow her gifts so unjustly: what, too, can a good man hope to obtain when he sees the best of men meeting with the worst fates.
peace-of-mind_section-16.plainEnglish: Now we come to a part of this topic that naturally makes us sad and worried. I'm talking about when good men meet terrible ends. When Socrates is forced to die in prison, when Rutilius has to live in exile, when Pompeius and Cicero have to offer their necks to the swords of their own followers, when the great Cato — that living picture of virtue — falls on his sword and destroys both himself and the republic. You can't help feeling grief that Fortune hands out her rewards so unfairly. What hope can a good man have when he sees the best people meeting the worst fates?

peace-of-mind_section-16.originalText: Well, but see how each of them endured his fate, and if they endured it bravely, long in your heart for courage as great as theirs; if they died in a womanish and cowardly manner, nothing was lost: either they deserved that you should admire their courage, or else they did not deserve that you should wish to imitate their cowardice: for what can be more shameful than that the greatest men should die so bravely as to make people cowards.
peace-of-mind_section-16.plainEnglish: But look at how each of them faced their fate. If they endured it bravely, then long for courage as great as theirs. If they died in a weak and cowardly way, nothing was lost. Either they earned your admiration for their courage, or they showed you exactly the kind of cowardice you shouldn't copy. After all, what could be more shameful than great men dying so bravely that it makes other people into cowards?

peace-of-mind_section-16.originalText: Let us praise one who deserves such constant praises, and say, "The braver you are the happier you are! You have escaped from all accidents, jealousies, diseases: you have escaped from prison: the gods have not thought you worthy of ill-fortune, but have thought that fortune no longer deserved to have any power over you": but when any one shrinks back in the hour of death and looks longingly at life, we must lay hands upon him.
peace-of-mind_section-16.plainEnglish: Let us praise someone who deserves endless praise, and say, 'The braver you are, the happier you are! You have escaped all accidents, jealousy, and disease. You have escaped from prison. The gods didn't think you deserved misfortune — they decided that fortune no longer deserved any power over you.' But when someone pulls back at the moment of death and looks longingly at life, we must take hold of them.

peace-of-mind_section-16.originalText: I will never weep for a man who dies cheerfully, nor for one who dies weeping: the former wipes away my tears, the latter by his tears makes himself unworthy that any should be shed for him. Shall I weep for Hercules because he was burned alive, or for Regulus because he was pierced by so many nails, or for Cato because he tore open his wounds a second time? All these men discovered how at the cost of a small portion of time they might obtain immortality, and by their deaths gained eternal life.
peace-of-mind_section-16.plainEnglish: I will never cry for a man who dies happily, or for one who dies crying. The cheerful one dries my tears. The weeping one makes himself unworthy of anyone's tears. Should I weep for Hercules because he was burned alive? Or for Regulus because he was pierced by so many nails? Or for Cato because he reopened his wounds a second time? All these men figured out how to trade a small bit of time for immortality. Through their deaths, they gained eternal life.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: It also proves a fertile source of troubles if you take pains to conceal your feelings and never show yourself to any one undisguised, but, as many men do, live an artificial life, in order to impose upon others: for the constant watching of himself becomes a torment to a man, and he dreads being caught doing something at variance with his usual habits, and, indeed, we never can be at our ease if we imagine that every one who looks at us is weighing our real value: for many things occur which strip people of their disguise, however reluctantly they may part with it, and even if all this trouble about oneself is successful, still life is neither happy nor safe when one always has to wear a mask.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: You'll also find endless trouble if you work hard to hide your true feelings and never let anyone see the real you. Many people live fake lives to impress others. But constantly watching yourself becomes torture. You're always afraid someone will catch you acting differently than usual. And we can never relax if we think everyone who looks at us is judging our worth. Many things happen that strip away our disguises, no matter how much we want to keep them on. Even if you succeed at fooling everyone, life is neither happy nor safe when you always have to wear a mask.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: But what pleasure there is in that honest straight-forwardness which is its own ornament, and which conceals no part of its character! Yet even this life, which hides nothing from any one runs some risk of being despised; for there are people who disdain whatever they come close to: but there is no danger of virtue's becoming contemptible when she is brought near our eyes, and it is better to be scorned for one's simplicity than to bear the burden of unceasing hypocrisy.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: But there's real joy in being honest and straightforward. This kind of life is beautiful on its own — it doesn't hide any part of who you are. Yet even this open way of living has some risk. Some people look down on anything they get too close to. But virtue can never become truly contemptible when people see it up close. It's better to be mocked for being simple than to carry the heavy burden of constant pretending.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Still, we must observe moderation in this matter, for there is a great difference between living simply and living slovenly. Moreover, we ought to retire a great deal into ourselves: for association with persons unlike ourselves upsets all that we had arranged, rouses the passions which were at rest, and rubs into a sore any weak or imperfectly healed place in our minds. Nevertheless we ought to mix up these two things, and to pass our lives alternately in solitude and among throngs of people; for the former will make us long for the society of mankind, the latter for that of ourselves, and the one will counteract the other: solitude will cure us when we are sick of crowds, and crowds will cure us when we are sick of solitude.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: Still, we need to be moderate about this. There's a big difference between living simply and living like a slob. We should spend a lot of time alone with ourselves. Being around people who are different from us disrupts everything we've organized. It stirs up emotions that were calm and irritates any weak or half-healed spots in our minds. But we should mix these two things together. We need to alternate between solitude and being around crowds. Solitude will make us miss other people. Crowds will make us miss being alone. Each one balances out the other. Solitude cures us when we're sick of crowds. Crowds cure us when we're sick of solitude.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Neither ought we always to keep the mind strained to the same pitch, but it ought sometimes to be relaxed by amusement. Socrates did not blush to play with little boys, Cato used to refresh his mind with wine after he had wearied it with application to affairs of state, and Scipio would move his triumphal and soldierly limbs to the sound of music, not with a feeble and halting gait, as is the fashion now-a-days, when we sway in our very walk with more than womanly weakness, but dancing as men were wont in the days of old on sportive and festal occasions, with manly bounds, thinking it no harm to be seen so doing even by their enemies. Men's minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest. We must not force crops from rich fields, for an unbroken course of heavy crops will soon exhaust their fertility, and so also the liveliness of our minds will be destroyed by unceasing labour, but they will recover their strength after a short period of rest and relief: for continuous toil produces a sort of numbness and sluggishness.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: We shouldn't always keep our minds stretched tight. Sometimes we need to relax with fun activities. Socrates wasn't embarrassed to play with children. Cato would refresh his mind with wine after tiring himself with government business. Scipio would move his victorious warrior's body to music — not with the weak, stumbling steps that are fashionable now, when we sway in our walking with more than feminine weakness. He danced the way men used to dance in the old days during celebrations, with strong, manly movements. He thought there was no shame in being seen this way, even by his enemies. Our minds need to relax. They come back stronger and more energetic after rest. We can't force crops from rich fields forever — constant heavy harvesting will quickly drain their fertility. In the same way, our minds lose their sharpness when we work them without stopping. But they regain their strength after a short period of rest and relief. Non-stop work creates a kind of numbness and dullness.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Men would not be so eager for this, if play and amusement did not possess natural attractions for them, although constant indulgence in them takes away all gravity and all strength from the mind: for sleep, also, is necessary for our refreshment, yet if you prolong it for days and nights together it will become death. There is a great difference between slackening your hold of a thing and letting it go. The founders of our laws appointed festivals, in order that men might be publicly encouraged to be cheerful, and they thought it necessary to vary our labours with amusements, and, as I said before, some great men have been wont to give themselves a certain number of holidays in every month, and some divided every day into play-time and work-time.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: People wouldn't want fun and games so much if these activities weren't naturally appealing. But if you indulge in them constantly, they drain all seriousness and strength from your mind. Sleep is necessary to refresh us, but if you sleep for days on end, you'll die. There's a big difference between loosening your grip on something and letting it go completely. The founders of our laws created festivals so people would be encouraged to celebrate in public. They knew we needed to break up our work with entertainment. As I mentioned before, some great men used to give themselves a certain number of holidays each month. Others divided every day into time for play and time for work.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Thus, I remember that great orator Asinius Pollio would not attend to any business after the tenth hour: he would not even read letters after that time for fear some new trouble should arise, but in those two hours used to get rid of the weariness which he had contracted during the whole day. Some rest in the middle of the day, and reserve some light occupation for the afternoon. Our ancestors, too, forbade any new motion to be made in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers divide their watches, and those who have just returned from active service are allowed to sleep the whole night undisturbed. We must humour our minds and grant them rest from time to time, which acts upon them like food, and restores their strength.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: I remember the great speaker Asinius Pollio had a firm rule: after the tenth hour, he wouldn't handle any business. He wouldn't even read his mail, worried that some new problem might come up. Instead, he used those two hours to shake off all the tiredness he'd built up during the day. Some people take a break in the middle of the day and save lighter work for the afternoon. Our ancestors also had a rule — no new business could be brought up in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers split up their watch duties, and those just back from active duty get to sleep through the entire night without interruption. We need to be kind to our minds and give them rest from time to time. Rest works on the mind like food — it restores our strength.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: It does good also to take walks out of doors, that our spirits may be raised and refreshed by the open air and fresh breeze: sometimes we gain strength by driving in a carriage, by travel, by change of air, or by social meals and a more generous allowance of wine: at times we ought to drink even to intoxication, not so as to drown, but merely to dip ourselves in wine: for wine washes away troubles and dislodges them from the depths of the mind, and acts as a remedy to sorrow as it does to some diseases. The inventor of wine is called Liber, not from the licence which he gives to our tongues, but because he liberates the mind from the bondage of cares, and emancipates it, animates it, and renders it more daring in all that it attempts.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: It's also good to take walks outside. Fresh air and a nice breeze lift our spirits and refresh us. Sometimes we get stronger by going for a drive, traveling, changing scenery, or sharing meals with friends and drinking more wine than usual. Sometimes we should even drink until we're drunk — not to drown our sorrows, but just to soak ourselves in wine. Wine washes away our troubles and pulls them up from deep in our minds. It works as medicine for sadness, just like it does for some illnesses. The god who invented wine is called Liber — not because wine loosens our tongues, but because it frees our minds from worry, breaks us out of mental chains, and makes us bolder in everything we try.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Yet moderation is wholesome both in freedom and in wine. It is believed that Solon and Arcesilaus used to drink deep. Cato is reproached with drunkenness: but whoever casts this in his teeth will find it easier to turn his reproach into a commendation than to prove that Cato did anything wrong: however, we ought not to do it often, for fear the mind should contract evil habits, though it ought sometimes to be forced into frolic and frankness, and to cast off dull sobriety for a while. If we believe the Greek poet, "it is sometimes pleasant to be mad"; again, Plato always knocked in vain at the door of poetry when he was sober; or, if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever been without a touch of insanity.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: But moderation is healthy in both freedom and wine. People say that Solon and Arcesilaus were heavy drinkers. Critics attack Cato for being a drunk. But anyone who tries to shame him for this will find it easier to turn their attack into praise than to prove Cato ever did anything truly wrong. Still, we shouldn't do this often. We don't want our minds to pick up bad habits. But sometimes we should force ourselves into playfulness and honesty. We should shake off boring seriousness for a while. If we believe the Greek poet, "it is sometimes pleasant to be mad." And Plato always knocked in vain at poetry's door when he was sober. Or if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever existed without a touch of madness.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: The mind cannot use lofty language, above that of the common herd, unless it be excited. When it has spurned aside the commonplace environments of custom, and rises sublime, instinct with sacred fire, then alone can it chant a song too grand for mortal lips: as long as it continues to dwell within itself it cannot rise to any pitch of splendour: it must break away from the beaten track, and lash itself to frenzy, till it gnaws the curb and rushes away bearing up its rider to heights whither it would fear to climb when alone.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: The mind cannot speak with power and beauty unless something stirs it up. It has to reject the ordinary world around it and rise up, filled with sacred fire. Only then can it create something too magnificent for human lips. As long as the mind stays comfortable and safe, it cannot achieve greatness. It must break away from the well-worn path. It must whip itself into a frenzy until it bites the bit and carries its rider to heights that would terrify it if it were climbing alone.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: I have now, my beloved Serenus, given you an account of what things can preserve peace of mind, what things can restore it to us, what can arrest the vices which secretly undermine it: yet be assured, that none of these is strong enough to enable us to retain so fleeting a blessing, unless we watch over our vacillating mind with intense and unremitting care.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: I've told you, my dear Serenus, what can protect peace of mind, what can bring it back when we lose it, and what can stop the vices that secretly eat away at it. But remember this: none of these methods is strong enough to help us keep such a fragile gift unless we guard our wavering mind with intense and constant attention.
